Colorado River Basin: End-to-End Data Pipeline, Relational Storage & Hydrologic Analysis #

Author: Douglas Schoch • Course: DAT1001: Introduction to Data Science (Colorado Mountain College)

Primary Sources: USGS NWIS Water Services, USBR Reclamation HydroData & RiverOps, USBR Natural Flow Workbook (1906–2024), Colorado DWR (CDSS)

Executive Summary & Research Question #

Under the 1922 Colorado River Compact and 1944 Mexican Water Treaty, statutory apportionments claim 16.50–17.50 MAF/yr (plus 1.26 MAF/yr in measured mainstem reservoir evaporation over CY 2005–2024 USBR CUL accounting), calibrated during an abnormally wet 1905–1922 window. Across the official 1922–2024 USBR Lees Ferry Natural Flow record (103 water years)—and especially since 2000—actual "wet water" falls chronically short of legal "paper water" claims.

This notebook is a self-contained technical submission explaining:

  1. How our automated ingestion pipeline queries live public APIs (Lee's Ferry, Lake Powell, Lake Mead, and basin tributaries),
  2. How data evolved from loose JSON files into normalized SQLite storage (data/colorado_river_basin.db) that compiles lightweight static JSON contracts (web/data/*.json),
  3. How GitHub Actions + GitHub Pages update and serve the static dashboard every 6 hours without a backend server, and
  4. How the portal's core Chart.js and D3.js visualizations are reproduced in Python using seaborn, matplotlib, and pandas.

1. Architecture: Data Pipeline, SQLite Storage & GitHub Pages + Actions Workflow #

A. Unidirectional Single Source of Truth (data/raw/ → SQLite → web/data/*.json) #

Early prototypes wrote API responses directly into standalone JSON files. Today the pipeline enforces strict unidirectional data provenance:

  1. Immutable Raw Archive (data/raw/ & data/raw/MANIFEST.csv): Preserves 26 original federal workbooks, compacts, USGS daily/statistics downloads, and USBR reservoir CSVs with recorded byte sizes and SHA-256 checksums.
  2. Persist in SQLite (data/colorado_river_basin.db): scripts/build_database.py, src/fetch_water_data.py, src/compute_rbi_and_sentinels.py, src/fetch_historical_portal_data.py, and src/fetch_replay_*.py normalize stations, live telemetry, 103-year USBR natural flow (annual_lees_ferry), CY 2005–2024 USBR CUL water budgets (water_budget_nodes, water_budget_meta), 74 daily Richards–Baker Flashiness stations (rbi_flashiness), and source_catalog.
  3. Compile Static JSON Contracts (scripts/export_sqlite_to_json.py → web/data/*.json): Exports all 10 non-GeoJSON JSON contracts (latest_metrics.json, portal_historical.json, seasonal_regimes.json, tributary_hydrology.json, station_hierarchy.json, historical_normals.json, water_budget.json, provenance_registry.json, replay_7d.json, replay_30d.json) directly from SQLite.

B. Serverless Hosting, CI Gates & Automation (GitHub Pages + GitHub Actions) #

Because GitHub Pages serves static files (HTML/CSS/JS/JSON) with zero server-side runtime, freshness is automated via GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/update_data.yml):

  • Schedule: cron: '0 */6 * * *' triggers every 6 hours (00:00, 06:00, 12:00, 18:00 UTC), plus manual workflow_dispatch runs.
  • Pipeline & Parity Gates: The runner executes fetch_water_data.py, fetch_historical_portal_data.py, fetch_replay_7d.py, fetch_replay_30d.py, scripts/export_sqlite_to_json.py, and scripts/data_smoke_test.py (verifying MANIFEST SHA-256, SQLite/JSON parity, 1937+ timeline start, water_budget closure, and claims register verification) before committing.
  • Commit & Deploy: Only after all smoke tests pass does github-actions[bot] commit updated data/colorado_river_basin.db and web/data/*.json to main, updating GitHub Pages.

2. Live Public API Ingestion Samples: Lee's Ferry, Lake Powell & Lake Mead #

Why These Three Stations Anchor the Basin #

  • Lee's Ferry (USGS #09380000): The statutory 1922 Compact dividing point between Upper and Lower Divisions (75.0 MAF over any rolling 10-year window) and the tailwater directly below Glen Canyon Dam.
  • Lake Powell (USBR Site 919): The Upper Basin's primary multi-year storage bank (24.32 MAF live capacity; minimum power pool 3,490 ft).
  • Lake Mead (USBR Site 921): The Lower Basin's primary storage bank (26.13 MAF live capacity; Tier 1 shortage trigger 1,075 ft, dead pool 895 ft).

Full Official API Documentation (Additional Fields Available) #

While our live dashboard extracts streamflow discharge (00060) and reservoir elevation/storage (49.csv / 17.csv), these public APIs expose many additional physical parameters (water temperature 00010, specific conductance 00095, precipitation 00045, reservoir inflows, turbine releases, evaporation, and power generation):

  • USGS Water Services Portal & Full Docs: waterservices.usgs.gov/docs/ ↗
  • USBR Upper Colorado HydroData Portal: usbr.gov/uc/water/hydrodata/ ↗ • Reservoir Site Map ↗
  • USBR Lower Colorado RiverOps Portal: usbr.gov/lc/riverops.html ↗
  • Colorado DWR (CDSS) REST API v2: dwr.state.co.us/Rest/GET/Help ↗

HEADERS = {'User-Agent': 'DAT1001-ColoradoRiverNotebook/1.0'}

def sample_lees_ferry_usgs():
    """Fetch live USGS IV (00060 discharge + 00065 gage height) for Lee's Ferry #09380000."""
    url = 'https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/iv/'
    params = {'sites': '09380000', 'parameterCd': '00060,00065', 'siteStatus': 'active', 'format': 'json'}
    try:
        r = requests.get(url, params=params, headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        out = {}
        for ts in r.json()['value']['timeSeries']:
            pcode = ts['variable']['variableCode'][0]['value']
            val = ts['values'][0]['value'][-1]
            out[pcode] = {'value': float(val['value']), 'datetime': val['dateTime']}
        return pd.DataFrame([{
            'station': "Lee's Ferry (#09380000)",
            'discharge_cfs': out.get('00060', {}).get('value'),
            'gage_height_ft': out.get('00065', {}).get('value'),
            'timestamp': out.get('00060', {}).get('datetime'),
            'source': 'LIVE USGS NWIS IV',
        }])
    except Exception:
        lm = json.load(open(os.path.join(WEB_DATA_DIR, 'latest_metrics.json')))
        rec = next(s for s in lm['streamflows'] if s['id'] == '09380000')
        return pd.DataFrame([{
            'station': rec['name'], 'discharge_cfs': rec['flow_cfs'],
            'gage_height_ft': None, 'timestamp': rec['timestamp'], 'source': 'LOCAL SNAPSHOT',
        }])

def sample_usbr_reservoir_csv(site_id, label, fallback_id):
    """Fetch official USBR HydroData daily elevation (49.csv) & storage (17.csv)."""
    u_elev = f'https://www.usbr.gov/uc/water/hydrodata/reservoir_data/{site_id}/csv/49.csv'
    u_stor = f'https://www.usbr.gov/uc/water/hydrodata/reservoir_data/{site_id}/csv/17.csv'
    try:
        re_ = requests.get(u_elev, headers=HEADERS, timeout=15); re_.raise_for_status()
        rs_ = requests.get(u_stor, headers=HEADERS, timeout=15); rs_.raise_for_status()
        df_e = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(re_.text), comment='#', names=['date', 'elevation_ft'], skiprows=1)
        df_s = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(rs_.text), comment='#', names=['date', 'storage_af'], skiprows=1)
        df = pd.merge(df_e, df_s, on='date').dropna()
        df['elevation_ft'] = pd.to_numeric(df['elevation_ft'], errors='coerce')
        df['storage_af'] = pd.to_numeric(df['storage_af'], errors='coerce')
        df['reservoir'] = label
        return df.dropna().tail(5)[['reservoir', 'date', 'elevation_ft', 'storage_af']]
    except Exception:
        lm = json.load(open(os.path.join(WEB_DATA_DIR, 'latest_metrics.json')))
        rec = next(r for r in lm['reservoirs'] if r['id'] == fallback_id)
        return pd.DataFrame([{
            'reservoir': label, 'date': rec['timestamp'][:10],
            'elevation_ft': rec['elevation_ft'], 'storage_af': rec['storage_af'],
        }])

print('--- Live USGS Sample: Lee\'s Ferry (#09380000) ---')
print(sample_lees_ferry_usgs().to_string(index=False))
print('\n--- Live USBR HDB Sample: Lake Powell (Site 919, last 5 days) ---')
print(sample_usbr_reservoir_csv(919, 'Lake Powell', 'lake_powell').to_string(index=False))
print('\n--- Live USBR HDB Sample: Lake Mead (Site 921, last 5 days) ---')
print(sample_usbr_reservoir_csv(921, 'Lake Mead', 'lake_mead').to_string(index=False))

4. Python (seaborn / matplotlib) Recreations of the Portal's Core Charts #

On the live website, these charts are rendered in JavaScript with Chart.js and D3.js. Here we recreate all six core analytical figures natively in Python using seaborn and matplotlib directly from the verified SQLite tables and JSON contracts.

Figure 1 — Official USBR Natural Flow vs. 16.5 MAF Compact Promises (1922–2024) #

Why we care: Proves quantitatively that the 1922 Compact's statutory paper promises (7.5 Upper + 7.5 Lower + 1.5 Mexico = 16.5 MAF/yr) exceed physical natural runoff in roughly two out of every three years—and 21 of 25 years since 2000.

In [4]: Python 3

sns.lineplot(data=df_compact, x='water_year', y='ten_year_rolling_mean_maf', ax=ax, color=CORRIDOR['ochre'], lw=2.2, label='10-Yr Rolling Mean Natural Flow')

Figure 2 & Figure 3 — Basin Storage Trajectory (1937–2026) & Dam-Era Seasonal Inflow vs. Release (WY 2000–2025) #

Why we care:

  • Figure 2 (Chart.js Overview Card 3 equivalent): Shows how Lake Mead (1937+ volume record) and Lake Powell (1963+) absorbed decades of over-allocation before declining from 55.8 MAF peak (EOY 1983 / Jul 1984, 93% capacity) to ~17.6 MAF (29.4% capacity today).
  • Figure 3 (Chart.js Overview Card 2 equivalent): Replaces idealized demand waves with real WY 2000–2025 USGS daily means—comparing gaged Lake Powell inflows (Cisco + Green River + San Juan) against Glen Canyon Dam releases (Lees Ferry #09380000), revealing a brief 87-day snowmelt refill window vs. 278 days of net drawdown.

ax2.set_xlabel('Year')
ax2.set_ylabel('Active Storage (MAF)')
ax2.set_ylim(0, 65)
ax2.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=8, frameon=True, facecolor='white')

# Figure 3: WY 2000-2025 Real Powell Inflow vs. Lees Ferry Release
sd = sr['supply_demand_mismatch']
df_sd = pd.DataFrame({'doy': sd['doy'], 'inflow_cfs': sd['supply_cfs'], 'release_cfs': sd['demand_cfs']})
sns.lineplot(data=df_sd, x='doy', y='inflow_cfs', ax=ax3, color=CORRIDOR['blue'], lw=2.0, label='Gaged Powell Inflow (Cisco + Green + SJ)')
sns.lineplot(data=df_sd, x='doy', y='release_cfs', ax=ax3, color=CORRIDOR['ochre'], ls='--', lw=2.0, label='Glen Canyon Release (Lees Ferry #09380000)')
ax3.fill_between(df_sd['doy'], df_sd['inflow_cfs'], df_sd['release_cfs'], where=(df_sd['inflow_cfs'] >= df_sd['release_cfs']), color=CORRIDOR['blue'], alpha=0.16, label=f"Refill ({sd['surplus_days']}d)")
ax3.fill_between(df_sd['doy'], df_sd['inflow_cfs'], df_sd['release_cfs'], where=(df_sd['inflow_cfs'] < df_sd['release_cfs']), color=CORRIDOR['red'], alpha=0.12, label=f"Drain ({sd['deficit_days']}d)")
month_starts = [1, 32, 60, 91, 121, 152, 182, 213, 244, 274, 305, 335]

ax3.set_xticklabels(['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr','May','Jun','Jul','Aug','Sep','Oct','Nov','Dec'], fontsize=8.5)
ax3.set_title('Figure 3: Dam-Era Seasonal Inflow vs. Release (WY 2000–2025)', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold', loc='left')
ax3.set_xlabel('Calendar Month')
ax3.set_ylabel('Mean Daily Discharge (cfs)')
ax3.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=7.8, frameon=True, facecolor='white')

Figure 4 — Why Flash Flood Headlines Mislead: Tributary Volume, Powell Canyon Shape & WY 2021 Event Proof #

Why we care: Recreates the three Chart.js panels of Tributary Hydrology (web/ml_analysis.html) from web/data/tributary_hydrology.json:

  1. Panel A (Flashiness vs. Volume): Across 10 years of raw daily USGS data (WY 2016–2025), snowmelt rivers (Cisco, Green, San Juan) deliver 99.2% of gaged Lake Powell inflow, while flashy desert tributaries (Dirty Devil, Escalante) deliver 0.78%.
  2. Panel B (Lake Powell Hypsometry): Because Glen Canyon is V-shaped, rising 1 ft at current drought elevation (3,541 ft) takes ~63,336 AF—less than half the 157,023 AF/ft required at full pool (3,700 ft). Thus identical storm runoff produces a taller headline elevation jump when the reservoir is low.
  3. Panel C (Rate vs. Volume): In WY 2021, the Dirty Devil peaked at 7,320 cfs (2021-09-02)—nearly matching Cisco's 8,300 cfs peak—yet its 3-day pulse delivered 16,171 AF (+3.06 inches on Lake Powell) vs. Cisco's 2.07 MAF.

Figure 5 & Figure 6 — True Daily Flashiness (SQLite) & Mass-Balanced 2005–2024 Water Budget (D3 Sankey Equivalent) #

Why we care:

  • Figure 5: Validates true daily WY 2016–2025 Richards–Baker Flashiness Index (RBI) stored in SQLite rbi_flashiness (74 USGS stations total; plotting 12 representative showcase stations), separating dam-regulated tailwaters (< 0.045), snowmelt rivers (0.045–0.150), and arid flash channels (>= 0.150).
  • Figure 6 (D3.js web/sankey.html equivalent): Queries SQLite water_budget_meta & water_budget_nodes for the CY/WY 2005–2024 13.89 MAF/yr USBR CUL macro accounting baseline (13.12 Lees Ferry natural flow + 0.39 Lower mainstem tribs + 0.26 5-reservoir storage drawdown + 0.12 closure residual = 13.89 MAF/yr balanced across states, Mexico, and mainstem reservoir evaporation).

5. Quality Control, Known Limitations & AI Usage Disclosure #

Engineering & Hydrologic Quality Controls #

  • Strict $Q$ vs. $V$ Separation: Instantaneous rates (cfs) and cumulative annual volumes (MAF/yr) are never conflated.
  • Zero Synthetic Curves: Every chart in this notebook and across the main analytical pages reads verified USGS nwis/dv/iv, USBR HydroData CSVs (919/921), or official USBR Natural Flow workbooks (1922–2024).
  • Audit Transparency: All 100+ human–AI work sessions, verification scripts, and screenshots are preserved verbatim in AI_LOG.md ↗, CHANGELOG.md ↗, and web/ai_complete_prompt_archive.html ↗.
